title: Decide what makes a private dinner feel exceptional to you
intro: Comparing luxury private dining experiences in Dubai starts with the kind of evening you want. Some guests value an interactive menu, others prefer discreet service and an intimate setting, and some want a relaxed meal with beautifully chosen ingredients. This guide explores those formats and the practical questions behind them. It is published by myCHEF to help you plan a suitable brief, rather than to present an independent provider ranking. The strongest choice connects your preferences with a menu, setting and service team that can deliver the agreed occasion.

sections.title: Look for coherence across the food, setting and service
paragraphs: A detailed tasting menu needs the time, workspace and staffing to serve it well. A generous sharing dinner needs a table and sequence that keep the experience comfortable. The level of formality should match the guests rather than being chosen only because it sounds impressive.

Explain what you would like to feel on the evening: relaxed, celebratory, curious or quietly looked after. Then discuss the practical choices that support it. A clear proposal should bring the menu and hospitality together, with any styling or other extras explicitly confirmed for your date.

sections.title: Match the service to the way your guests gather
paragraphs: Some occasions revolve around conversation at one table; others work better when guests move around and eat at their own pace. Describe how you imagine the gathering before choosing individual dishes. Food that is comfortable to eat standing may need different portions and presentation from a meal designed for a seated place setting.

Sharing service can encourage conversation, while plated courses create a more defined sequence. A mixed format may begin with small bites and move to a seated main course. Each option has implications for staff, crockery and the kitchen, so discuss the complete flow rather than deciding the menu and service separately.

Think about the guests who may need a quieter seat, an earlier meal or a simple alternative. A considerate arrangement makes them part of the occasion without requiring a complicated last-minute change. Once the format is clear, the chef can recommend dishes that suit it and the team can price the practical support needed.

link.label: Discuss the style of your occasion

sections.title: Make the chef’s craft part of the conversation
paragraphs: A chef's table experience brings preparation and explanation closer to the guests. It suits people who enjoy hearing about ingredients, asking questions and watching the finishing touches. Tell us how interactive you want the meal to be, because some groups enjoy detailed conversation while others prefer a short introduction and more time together.

The kitchen and seating arrangement shape what is possible. Guests need a comfortable view without crowding the working area, and the chef needs room to cook safely and serve smoothly. A domestic kitchen may support a different style of interaction from a dedicated counter, so share photographs before the format is agreed.

A tasting sequence should feel balanced rather than simply long. Discuss portion sizes, dietary variations and the overall pace. If guests want different levels of detail, the chef can keep explanations concise and invite questions. The result should be an engaging dinner with excellent food at its centre, not a demonstration that leaves the meal waiting.

sections.title: Choose courses that belong together
paragraphs: A memorable dinner menu is more than a list of favourite dishes. Think about how the courses follow one another: a fresh beginning, a satisfying main course and a finish that complements what came before. Repeating the same rich ingredient or cooking style throughout can make a meal feel heavier than intended, even when each dish is good on its own.

Share your must-have dishes and let the chef recommend the supporting courses. If a particular main course is the centrepiece, the starter and dessert can be chosen to balance it. The menu should also respect the kitchen and service team, especially when several plates need to reach the table together.

Consider the pace you want. A relaxed family gathering, a birthday dinner and an interactive tasting menu may all use different course structures. Agreeing the format early makes it easier to discuss portions, staffing and timing. The most persuasive menu is one that sounds enjoyable to your guests and can be delivered comfortably in the setting.

sections.title: Make the table work as well as it looks
paragraphs: A beautiful table should still leave room to eat comfortably. Consider the number of plates, glasses and serving dishes before deciding on flowers or decorative pieces. A sharing menu needs space in the centre; a plated menu may need room for several pieces of cutlery or a separate bread plate. The menu and table layout should be planned together.

Check what is available at the property and what needs to be arranged. Crockery, serving platters, linen and glassware are not interchangeable with kitchen equipment, and they should not be assumed to be included unless your proposal says so. Tell the team if you want a particular style, colour palette or level of formality.

Lighting and access matter, too. Guests need to see the food, and staff need a safe route between the table and kitchen. A simple, thoughtfully arranged setting can feel more welcoming than an overcrowded display. Confirm setup and clear-down responsibilities so the presentation remains practical throughout the occasion.

link.label: Discuss your table and service requirements

sections.title: Give every person in the service a clear role
paragraphs: Cooking, carrying plates, pouring drinks and clearing a table are different jobs. For a quiet household visit, you may need only a chef. For an occasion with several courses or guests arriving together, an assistant or service professional can help the kitchen and dining area run at the right pace. Staffing should follow the work, rather than a fixed assumption based only on headcount.

Discuss who will greet guests, replenish water, serve each course and clear used plates. If the chef is expected to do all of those tasks while cooking, the menu and timing need to allow for it. Extra support can be especially useful when the kitchen is far from the dining table or the meal involves several dietary variations.

Your proposal should identify the included roles and service hours. Additional hospitality, equipment and event coordination should be agreed as part of the scope. That clarity lets everyone focus on their responsibilities and gives you a more relaxed experience as host.

photo.alt: A private dining table set with linen, flowers and candlelight

sections.title: Let ingredient choices support the cooking
paragraphs: A menu should be built around ingredients that can be sourced to the required standard for the date. If you have a particular fish, cut of meat or specialist product in mind, mention it early. Availability, size and price can influence whether the original dish is practical or whether an alternative would produce a better result.

Agree how substitutions will be handled. Some households are comfortable with the chef choosing a similar vegetable; others want to approve any change. Essential dietary requirements should never be treated as interchangeable preferences. A substitution that affects those requirements needs specific discussion before it is used.

There is also value in keeping a few menu decisions flexible. A well-chosen alternative can preserve the balance of a meal without forcing the chef to use an unsuitable ingredient simply because it appeared in an early draft. Your final menu and proposal should make the agreed choices clear, including any premium items that affect the overall price.
